rationale: B wins because it puts the real story where a skeptical education editor will put it: evidence standards before classroom scale. "Khan Academy's AI tutor reaches 1 million more students before the research is in" is sharper than A's "An AI tutor's own pilot data: regular users gained the equivalent of extra weeks of learning," which still lets Khan's internal metric drive the bus. A is usable, but B is less likely to walk a founder into the first reporter reply with the headline already overclaimed.
gaps_in_A: "A nonprofit is giving an AI tutor to teachers for free while the rest of ed-tech charges per seat" asserts a market comparison the update does not supply. Good instinct, bad headline discipline.
"one of the largest AI-tutoring deployments" is an unproven comparative claim. The update gives 30 districts and an estimated 1 million additional students, not a ranking.
"regular users gained the equivalent of extra weeks of learning" puts the internal, non-peer-reviewed result too cleanly in headline position. "By Khan's own measure" should not be an afterthought.
A misses B's sharper usage trap: whether "1 million additional students" means actual use, eligible students, seats, or district enrollment.
gaps_in_B: "a nonprofit with unusual credibility" imports reputation that is not in the update. True-sounding is not the same as sourced.
"The prevailing belief is that a nonprofit's free tool sidesteps the scrutiny applied to commercial edtech" invents a consensus just to knock it down. Cut the fake straw man.
"competitors sell" and "the same capability is a paid product elsewhere" are unsupported category claims. The proof note helps, but the headline still asserts what the facts do not give.

"I have no current news signal for this rollout" is muddy at best and wrong at worst. The supplied peg is the current rollout plus publication of classroom results; if you mean no outside news peg, say that.
